chapter.name: A Peek Beyond the Point
chapter.blurb: Decimal fractions: tenths/hundredths, place value, comparing and locating decimals, unit conversions, addition/subtraction, and estimation.

scope: Read/write a length as a mixed tenths quantity (e.g. 3 4/10) and convert to pure tenths (34/10)
Add and subtract quantities in tenths, regrouping across the whole-number boundary
Read/write a quantity combining tenths and hundredths (e.g. 4 4/10 5/100) and convert between forms
Add and subtract quantities in tenths and hundredths together, borrowing across places
Explain the place-value extension: each place past the point is 10x smaller than the one before it
Write a quantity in decimal notation and read it aloud digit-by-digit (7.05 = "seven point zero five")
Convert between "N tenths/hundredths" phrasing and decimal form (234 tenths = 23.4)
Convert between mm/cm/m, g/kg, and paise/rupee using decimal notation
Recognise trailing zeros don't change a decimal's value, but a zero right after the point does
Locate a decimal on a number line by zooming into successive segments
Compare two decimals digit-by-digit from the most significant place
Identify which of several decimals is closest to a target value
Add and subtract decimals with the standard column method, carrying/borrowing across the point
Identify and extend a decimal number sequence/pattern
Estimate a sum/difference of two decimals by bounding with their whole-number parts
Recognise that clock time and cricket overs LOOK decimal but aren't true base-10 decimals
Multiplication and division of decimals -- Not introduced anywhere in this chapter -- covered later in Part II Ch 4 "Another Peek Beyond the Point"
Rounding a decimal to a given decimal place -- Chapter 1 covered rounding whole numbers; this chapter never extends rounding to decimals
Recurring/repeating decimals -- Every example is a terminating decimal
Converting a general fraction (e.g. 1/3, 1/7) to decimal form -- Figure-it-Out only covers denominators 2, 4, 5 (clean terminating cases); non-terminating conversions are never attempted
Negative decimal numbers -- Every example is a positive real-world quantity (length, weight, money)
Compare two decimals digit by digit from the highest place value, and find which of several decimals is closest to a target value
Find the constant change in a decimal sequence and write its next terms

concepts.name: Reading & writing tenths and hundredths
concepts.description: Splitting a unit into tenths, and tenths into hundredths, to represent and convert precise measurements.
concepts.idea: A unit split into 10 equal parts gives tenths; each tenth split into 10 gives hundredths. A length like 3 4/10 can also be written as 34 one-tenths, or with tenths and hundredths together like 4 4/10 5/100.
concepts.rule: 10 tenths = 1 unit; 10 hundredths = 1 tenth. Convert between mixed and pure fractional-part forms by multiplying/dividing by 10.

concepts.name: Decimal place value and notation
concepts.description: The decimal point as an extension of the Indian place-value system to fractional parts.
concepts.idea: The decimal point extends the Indian place-value system to the right: each place past the point is 10 times smaller than the one before it (tenths, hundredths, thousandths).
concepts.rule: 70.5 = 7x10 + 0x1 + 5x1/10. Read digit-by-digit after the point (7.05 = "seven point zero five"), never as one big number.
concepts.example: 705 (7 hundreds+5 ones), 70.5 (7 tens+5 tenths), 7.05 (7 ones+5 hundredths) -- same digits, three different values.

concepts.name: Trailing zeros and equivalent decimal forms
concepts.description: When adding zeros to a decimal changes its value and when it does not.
concepts.idea: Adding zeros to the right end of a decimal doesn't change its value, but adding a zero between the point and the first digit does.
concepts.example: Sonu and Zara's disagreement: 0.2, 0.20 and 0.200 are all equal; 0.02 is ten times smaller.

concepts.name: Locating and comparing decimals
concepts.description: Placing decimals on a number line by zooming, and comparing them digit by digit.
concepts.idea: A decimal is located on a number line by zooming into successively smaller segments. Two decimals are compared digit by digit from the most significant place until a difference is found.
concepts.rule: Compare units first, then tenths, then hundredths, etc. -- the first place where digits differ decides which number is greater.
concepts.example: 6.456 vs 6.465: same units and tenths, but 5 hundredths < 6 hundredths, so 6.456 < 6.465.

concepts.name: Unit conversions using decimals
concepts.description: mm/cm/m, g/kg, and paise/rupee conversions expressed as decimal fractions.
concepts.idea: mm-to-cm, cm-to-m, g-to-kg and paise-to-rupee conversions are all decimal-fraction relationships (1 smaller unit = a tenth, hundredth or thousandth of the bigger one).

concepts.name: Addition and subtraction of decimals
concepts.description: Column addition and subtraction of decimal numbers, including carrying and borrowing across the point.
concepts.idea: Decimals add and subtract with the same column method as whole numbers, carrying/borrowing across the decimal point when a place value overflows (e.g. 10 hundredths becomes 1 tenth).
concepts.rule: Align decimal points, then add/subtract column by column right to left, carrying or borrowing as needed.

concepts.name: Estimating sums and differences of decimals
concepts.description: Bounding a decimal sum/difference using the whole-number parts of the two numbers.
concepts.idea: The sum of two decimals (each with a fractional part between 0 and 1) is always greater than the sum of their whole-number parts, and less than that sum plus 2.
concepts.rule: whole1 + whole2 < sum < whole1 + whole2 + 2 (since each fractional part is less than 1).
concepts.example: 25.936 + 8.202: sum is greater than 25+8=33 and less than 25+1+8+1=35.

concepts.name: Recognising non-decimal "decimal-look-alike" notation
concepts.description: Real-world quantities written with a point that are not true base-10 decimals, like clock time and cricket overs.
concepts.idea: Some real quantities are written with a point but are NOT base-10 decimals -- clock time (hours.tenths-of-an-hour, where each tenth is 6 minutes) and cricket overs (X.Y means X overs and Y balls, out of 6, not tenths).
concepts.rule: Before treating a "N.M" quantity as a decimal, check whether its unit actually subdivides into 10 -- an hour does not (60 min), and an over does not (6 balls).
concepts.example: 4.5 hours post noon = 4:30, not 4:05 or 4:50. "Overs left: 5.5" = 5 overs + 5 balls, not 5 overs 3 balls.

concepts.name: Closest decimals and decimal sequences
concepts.description: Comparing decimals digit by digit, finding the decimal closest to a target, and finding the change in a decimal sequence to extend it.
concepts.idea: Comparing place by place from the highest place tells which decimal is greater, and closeness to a target is the size of the difference, not the number of digits.
concepts.rule: Compare from the highest place; the first place where the digits differ decides. The closest decimal is the one with the smallest difference from the target. In a sequence, subtract neighbouring terms to find the change.
concepts.example: 1.01 is closest to 1 among 0.9, 1.1, 1.01 and 1.11, because it is 1/100 away while 0.9 is 10/100 away.
